source: Marqu - The Hebrew Gospel of Mark v1.2

verses.translation: This{H2088} is the good-news{H1309} of Yeshua{H3442} the Anointed{H4899}, son{H1121} of God{H433}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בשורה (besorah, H1309 — 'good tidings'), the OT herald-word for a messenger's good report (2 Sam 18:20,27; 2 Kgs 7:9; Isa 52:7). Greek εὐαγγέλιον is a semantic rendering of this Hebrew concept.

Uses אלוה (eloah, H433) — the singular form of God found primarily in Job (41 times) and in Deut 32:15,17; Hab 3:3. A back-translator from Greek θεοῦ would use the common אלהים (Elohim, H430), not this rare poetic singular.
greek_deviations: Some Greek manuscripts omit υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ ('Son of God'). The Hebrew includes it.
translation_notes: 'Good-news' for besorah rather than 'gospel' — preserving the Hebrew word's OT meaning of a messenger's good report.

verses.translation: As it is written{H3789} in Yeshayah{H3470} the prophet{H5030}, he said{H559}: See{H2009}! I send{H7971} my messenger{H4397} before your face{H6440}, who shall clear{H6437} your way{H1870} before you{H6440}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלאכי (malachi — 'my messenger', H4397) — the word that forms the prophet Malachi's name. Quoting Malachi 3:1, the Hebrew preserves the possessive suffix that connects the messenger directly to the prophetic name. Greek ἄγγελόν μου ('my messenger/angel') obscures this wordplay.

Uses שיפנה (she-yifneh — 'who shall clear/turn', H6437) from the root פנה ('to turn/clear'). Greek κατασκευάσει ('shall prepare/construct') is a different concept — 'construct' vs. 'clear away obstacles.' A back-translator from Greek would use יכין ('shall prepare'), not יפנה.
greek_deviations: Both Hebrew and Greek attribute the combined quotation (Mal 3:1 + Isa 40:3) to Isaiah alone.
translation_notes: 'Clear' for yifneh captures the root פנה (to turn aside/clear) — the herald clears the road of obstacles, not merely 'prepares' it.
textual_notes: Malachi 3:1: הִנְנִי שֹׁלֵחַ מַלְאָכִי וּפִנָּה דֶרֶךְ לְפָנָי — 'Behold I send my messenger, and he shall clear the way before me.' The Hebrew Gospel preserves the Malachi text closely.

verses.translation: A voice{H6963} calls{H7121} in the wilderness{H4057}, saying{H559}: Prepare{H3559} the way{H1870} of the Master{H113}! Make straight{H3474} the paths{H1870} of the Master{H113}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses האדון (ha-Adon, H113 — 'the Master/Lord'), the human title of authority (Gen 18:12, 42:30), where the Masoretic Isaiah 40:3 has יהוה (YHWH). Greek κυρίου ('Lord') could represent either. The Hebrew Gospel's choice of Adon rather than YHWH allows the verse to apply to Yeshua as master without directly equating him with the divine name.

Uses ישרות (yesharot — 'straight things', from H3474 ישר) — the feminine plural adjective. Isaiah 40:3 has יַשְּׁרוּ (yashru — imperative 'make straight'). The Hebrew Gospel uses a variant form of the same root, confirming awareness of the Isaiah source but with independent word choice.
translation_notes: 'Master' for Adon (H113) — distinguishing this from YHWH. Adon is the title of human lordship and authority.
textual_notes: Isaiah 40:3: קוֹל קוֹרֵא בַּמִּדְבָּר פַּנּוּ דֶּרֶךְ יְהוָה יַשְּׁרוּ בָּעֲרָבָה מְסִלָּה לֵאלֹהֵינוּ — 'A voice cries in the wilderness: clear the way of YHWH, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.'

verses.translation: Yochanan{H3110} was{H1961} in the wilderness{H4057} immersing{H2881} and proclaiming{H1875} an immersion of repentance{H8666} for atonement{H3722} of iniquities{H5771}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses טובל (tovel — 'immerser', H2881) — from the root טבל describing full-body ritual immersion (2 Kgs 5:14 — Naaman 'dipped' seven times in the Yarden; Lev 14:6). The Hebrew term carries the full OT ritual-purity framework.

CRITICAL: Uses כפרת (kaparat — 'atonement', from H3722 כפר) — the Yom Kippur vocabulary. Greek ἄφεσιν ('forgiveness/release') is far weaker. The Hebrew frames immersion as atonement ritual; the Greek frames it as mere forgiveness. A back-translator from Greek would use מחילה ('pardon') or סליחה ('forgiveness'), not the Levitical atonement term כפרה.

Uses תשובה (teshuvah — 'repentance/return', H8666, from שוב — 'to return'). This is the Hebrew concept of turning back to God, not merely changing one's mind. Greek μετάνοια ('change of mind') focuses on mental transformation; Hebrew focuses on directional return.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'atonement of iniquities' (כפרת עונות). Greek: 'forgiveness of sins' (ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν). Different theological framing — Levitical atonement vs. legal remission.
translation_notes: 'Atonement' for kaparat — preserving the Yom Kippur connection. The immersion is framed as a priestly atonement act.
'Repentance' for teshuvah, though the Hebrew literally means 'return' — the act of turning back to God's path.

verses.translation: And all{H3605} those from the kingdom{H4467} of Yehudah{H3063} and Yerushalayim{H3389} went out{H3318} to him, and he immersed{H2881} them in the river{H5104} Yarden{H3383}, and they confessed{H3034} their iniquities{H5771}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ממלכות יהודה ('from the kingdom of Yehudah', H4467) — a political-territorial designation. Greek πᾶσα ἡ Ἰουδαία χώρα ('all the Judean region'). The Hebrew frames Judah as a kingdom (malkhut), not a region (chora). A back-translator from Greek would use ארץ יהודה ('land of Judea') or מחוז ('district'), not 'kingdom.'

Uses מתודים (mitvadim — 'confessing', from H3034 ידה) — the Yom Kippur confession verb (Lev 16:21 — the priest 'confesses' all the iniquities of Israel over the scapegoat). Greek ἐξομολογούμενοι ('confessing') is a direct equivalent, but the Hebrew carries the Day of Atonement ritual context.
translation_notes: 'Kingdom' for malkhut preserves the political framing — Judah as a sovereign entity, not merely a geographic region.

verses.translation: And Yochanan{H3110} was{H1961} clothed{H3847} in skins{H5785} of camels{H1581}, and girded{H2296} around{H5439} the loins{H4975} with a girdle of leather{H5785}, and eating{H398} locusts{H2284} and honey{H1706} of the wilderness.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עורות גמלים ('skins of camels', H5785) — meaning hides. Greek τρίχας καμήλου ('camel hair'). The Hebrew says 'skins' (hides); the Greek says 'hair.' A back-translator from Greek would write שער גמלים ('camel hair'), not עורות ('skins'). This may preserve a more primitive description of the prophet's garb.
Uses דבש מדבריי ('wilderness honey') — specifying the source. Greek μέλι ἄγριον ('wild honey') specifies the quality. Hebrew identifies the terrain; Greek identifies the category.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'skins of camels' (hides). Greek: 'camel hair.' Different material.
textual_notes: The description echoes Elijah in 2 Kings 1:8: אִישׁ בַּעַל שֵׂעָר וְאֵזוֹר עוֹר אָזוּר בְּמָתְנָיו — 'a hairy man with a leather belt around his waist.' Yochanan is portrayed as the returning Elijah (Mal 4:5).

verses.translation: And he proclaimed{H1875} and said{H559}: One mightier{H2389} than I comes{H935} after me{H310}, whose sandal{H5275} strap{H8288} I am not worthy to loose{H2502}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לחלוץ (lachalutz — 'to loose/remove', H2502) — the same verb used in the levirate marriage ceremony where the widow removes (חלץ) the sandal (Deut 25:9-10, Ruth 4:7-8). Greek λῦσαι ('to untie') is generic. The Hebrew verb carries the legal overtone of the sandal-removal rite, implying Yochanan is unworthy even to perform this legal act for the Coming One. A back-translator from Greek would use להתיר ('to untie'), not the levirate-ceremony verb חלץ.
greek_deviations: Greek: κύψας λῦσαι ('stooping down to untie'). Hebrew has no 'stooping down' — only 'to loose.' The Greek adds the physical posture.
translation_notes: 'Loose' for chalutz preserves the sandal-removal ceremony connection.

verses.translation: I{H589} immerse{H2881} you in water{H4325}; he shall immerse{H2881} you from the Holy{H6918} Spirit{H7307}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses the preposition מ (min — 'from') in מהקדוש רוח ('from the Holy Spirit'). Greek ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ uses ἐν ('in/with'). The Hebrew preposition implies the Spirit as the source of immersion; the Greek implies the Spirit as the medium. A back-translator from Greek would write ברוח הקדש ('in/with the Holy Spirit'), not מ ('from').

Word order הקדוש רוח ('the-Holy Spirit') differs from the standard OT construct רוח הקדש ('spirit of holiness', Isa 63:10-11, Ps 51:13). This adjective-before-noun pattern may reflect later Hebrew syntax.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the Holy Spirit' (מ — 'from'). Greek: 'in/with the Holy Spirit' (ἐν — 'in'). Different preposition, different theology.
translation_notes: 'From' for the preposition מ, preserving the Hebrew source-origin sense.

verses.translation: And it came to pass{H6213} in those days{H3117} that Yeshua{H3442} the Natsri came{H935} from the city{H5892} of Galil{H1551}, and was immersed{H2881} in the river{H5104} Yarden{H3383} by Yochanan{H3110}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נצרי (Natsri — 'the Nazarene') as an epithet-title rather than a geographic origin. Greek ἀπὸ Ναζαρὲτ τῆς Γαλιλαίας ('from Nazareth of Galilee') treats it as geography. The Hebrew uses it as a title — 'Yeshua the Natsri' — similar to prophetic or clan designations.

Uses ונעשה (vena'aseh — 'and it came to pass', H6213) — a narrative formula using the root עשה ('to do/make') rather than the classical ויהי (vayehi — 'and it was'). This is a later Hebrew narrative style.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the city of Galil.' Greek: 'from Nazareth of Galilee.' The Hebrew omits Nazareth as a place name.

verses.translation: And immediately as he came out{H3318} from the water{H4325}, he saw{H7200} the heavens{H8064} opened{H6605}, and the Holy{H6918} Spirit{H7307} descending{H3381} upon him like the form{H1823} of a dove{H3123}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כדמות (kidmut — 'like the form/likeness of', H1823) — the same word from Genesis 1:26 ('in our likeness — דמות') and Ezekiel's throne visions (Ezek 1:5,10,22,26). Greek ὡς περιστεράν ('like a dove') is a simple comparison. The Hebrew word implies a visionary form — an Ezekiel-like apparition — not a simple simile. A back-translator from Greek would use כמו ('like'), not the theologically loaded דמות.

Uses נפתחו השמים ('the heavens were opened') — echoing Ezekiel 1:1 verbatim: וְנִפְתְּחוּ הַשָּׁמַיִם ('and the heavens were opened'). The Hebrew Gospel uses the identical passive form, connecting Yeshua's experience to Ezekiel's prophetic inauguration.
greek_deviations: Greek: σχιζομένους τοὺς οὐρανούς ('the heavens being torn/split'). Hebrew: השמים נפתחו ('the heavens were opened'). Different imagery — 'torn' (violent) vs. 'opened' (gentle). The Hebrew matches Ezekiel; the Greek is more dramatic.
translation_notes: 'Form' for demut preserves the Genesis/Ezekiel visionary language.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 1:1 — 'The heavens were opened (נפתחו השמים) and I saw visions of God.' The Hebrew Mark uses Ezekiel's exact inauguration formula.

verses.translation: And a voice{H6963} came{H6213} in the heavens{H8064}, saying{H559}: You are my son{H1121}; very{H3966} pleasing{H6149} to me, and beloved{H157}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ערב (arev — 'pleasing/sweet', H6149) — a sensory word describing sweetness to the senses (Ps 104:34 'May my meditation be sweet — יֶעֱרַב — to him'; Jer 31:26; Mal 3:4). Greek εὐδόκησα ('I am well-pleased') is cognitive. The Hebrew is sensory — the son is sweet/pleasing; the Greek is volitional. A back-translator from Greek would use רציתי ('I desired'), not the sensory ערב.
Uses אתהו (at'hu — emphatic 'you are he') — a uniquely Hebrew emphatic pronoun combining אתה+הוא. This emphatic identification has no Greek equivalent; Greek σὺ εἶ ('you are') is simpler.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'pleasing to me and beloved' (two qualities). Greek: ἐν σοὶ εὐδόκησα ('in you I am well-pleased'). Different structure — Hebrew gives two attributes; Greek gives one statement of approval.
translation_notes: 'Pleasing' for arev captures the sensory Hebrew quality rather than the cognitive 'well-pleased.'
textual_notes: Echoes Psalm 2:7 ('You are my son') and Isaiah 42:1 ('my chosen, in whom my soul delights'). The Hebrew combines both sources.

verses.translation: And immediately the Holy{H6918} Spirit{H7307} led{H5090} him into the wilderness{H4057}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses נהגו (nahagu — 'led him', H5090) — a pastoral verb for leading flocks (Gen 31:18, Isa 11:6) and guiding gently (Isa 49:10). Greek ἐκβάλλει ('casts out/drives out') is violent — the same word used for casting out demons. A back-translator from Greek would use גרש ('drove out') or השליך ('cast'). The Hebrew Spirit gently leads like a shepherd; the Greek Spirit violently drives.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'led him' (gentle guidance). Greek: 'drives him out' (forceful expulsion). Fundamentally different portrayals of the Spirit's action.
translation_notes: 'Led' for nahag captures the pastoral Hebrew sense — the Spirit guides like a shepherd, not drives like an exorcist.

verses.translation: There{H8033} he fasted{H6031} forty{H705} days{H3117} and forty{H705} nights{H3915}, and the Adversary{H7854} tested{H5254} him. And he stood{H5975} there among{H996} the beasts{H929}, and the messengers{H4397} ministered{H8334} to him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses התענה (hit'aneh — 'fasted/afflicted himself', H6031) — from ענה, the Yom Kippur verb: 'you shall afflict your souls' (תְּעַנּוּ — Lev 16:29,31; 23:27,32). Greek πειραζόμενος focuses on temptation only. The Hebrew adds a Yom Kippur-style self-affliction absent from the Greek.

Uses משרתים (mesharetim — 'ministering', H8334) — the Levitical service verb used of priests and Levites serving in the sanctuary (Num 3:6, 1 Sam 2:11, Ezek 44:11). Greek διηκόνουν ('served/waited on') is generic table service. The Hebrew frames angelic ministry as priestly/Levitical service.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'forty nights' (ומ' לילה) — matching the Moses template (Ex 34:28). Greek mentions only 'forty days.'
translation_notes: 'Fasted' for hit'aneh, though the Hebrew word means 'afflicted himself' — the broader Yom Kippur concept of self-denial.
textual_notes: The 'forty days and forty nights' directly parallels Moses (Ex 24:18, 34:28) and Elijah (1 Kgs 19:8). The Hebrew frames Yeshua's testing in the Torah/Prophets template.

verses.translation: And after{H310} Yochanan{H3110} was{H1961} bound{H631}, Yeshua{H3442} came{H935} into Galil{H1551}, proclaiming{H1875} the word{H1697} of God{H410}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אסור (asur — 'bound/imprisoned', H631) — from the root אסר, used of binding prisoners (Gen 42:24, Judg 16:21, 2 Kgs 25:7). Greek παραδοθῆναι ('was handed over/delivered up') carries theological weight of divine providence. The Hebrew is concrete and physical — Yochanan was bound in chains; the Greek is theological — he was delivered up. A back-translator from Greek would use נמסר ('was handed over'), not אסור ('was bound').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the word of God' (דבר האל). Greek: τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ θεοῦ ('the gospel of God'). Different content description — 'word' vs. 'gospel.'

verses.translation: And saying{H559}: The time{H6256} has come{H935}! The kingdom{H4467} of heaven{H8064} — make{H6213} repentance{H8666} and believe{H539} the word{H1697} of God{H410}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses ממלכות שמים ('kingdom of heaven', H4467+H8064) — the circumlocution avoiding the divine name, identical to Matthew's consistent מלכות השמים. Greek has βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ('kingdom of God'). Greek Mark NEVER uses 'kingdom of heaven'; only 'kingdom of God.' The Hebrew Gospel uses the Jewish reverence pattern. A back-translator from Greek would write מלכות האל, not מלכות שמים.
Uses עשו תשובה ('make repentance' — lit. 'do teshuvah'). The verb+noun combination is a native Hebrew idiom for the act of returning. Greek μετανοεῖτε ('repent/change your mind') is a single verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'kingdom of heaven.' Greek: 'kingdom of God.' The Hebrew uses the Jewish reverential circumlocution.
Hebrew: 'the word of God' (דבר האל). Greek: τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ ('the gospel'). Different object of belief.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} was walking{H1980} with others in Galil{H1551}, and he saw{H7200} Shimon{H8095} and Andri his brother{H251} casting the nets{H7568} in the sea{H3220}, for they were fishermen{H1771}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: 'walking with others' (והולך ישוע ואחרים). Greek: 'passing alongside the Sea of Galilee' (παράγων παρὰ τὴν θάλασσαν). The Hebrew has Yeshua walking with companions already; the Greek has him alone by the sea. Different narrative setup.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in Galil' (no mention of the sea in the itinerary). Greek: 'beside the Sea of Galilee.' Different framing of the scene.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559} to them: Come{H935} and walk{H1980} after me{H310}, and I will make{H6213} you fishermen{H1771} of men{H376}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לכו אחרי ('walk after me') — the Hebrew discipleship idiom הלך אחרי (halach acharei), used for following God (Deut 13:5, 1 Kgs 14:8) and prophets (1 Kgs 19:20-21 — Elisha 'went after' Elijah). Greek δεῦτε ὀπίσω μου ('come behind me') is less idiomatic. The Hebrew carries the Elijah-Elisha prophetic call pattern.
translation_notes: 'Walk after me' rather than 'follow me' preserves the Hebrew idiom of discipleship as walking in another's path.

verses.translation: And they immediately left{H5800} the nets{H7568} and walked{H1980} after him{H310}.
And going{H1980} a little{H4592} further, he saw{H7200} Yaakov{H3290} and Yochanan{H3110}, sons{H1121} of Zavdi{H2067}, in a small{H6996} boat, mending their nets{H7568}.
And immediately he called{H7121} them, and they left{H5800} their father{H1} Zavdi{H2067} in the small{H6996} boat.

greek_deviations: Greek adds μετὰ τῶν μισθωτῶν ('with the hired workers') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew scene is starker: the sons leave their father alone.

verses.translation: And they walked{H1980} after him and entered{H935} Kfar Nachum, and immediately on the Shabbat{H7676} they entered{H935} the house of assembly, and he was teaching{H3925} them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כפר נחום ('village of Nachum') — preserving the Hebrew meaning: כפר ('village') + נחום ('comfort'). Greek Καφαρναούμ is a transliteration that obscures the meaning.
Uses בית הכנסת ('house of assembly') — the full Hebrew construct phrase. Greek συναγωγή is a single compressed word that originates from this Hebrew concept.

verses.translation: And all{H3605} were astonished{H8539} at the instruction{H4148}, for he was{H1961} teaching{H3925} them like a master{H1167} of power{H3581}, not like the wise-ones of the law.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מוסר (musar, H4148 — 'instruction/discipline') — the Proverbs wisdom-word (Prov 1:2,7,8; 4:1,13; 8:33). Greek διδαχή ('teaching/doctrine') is generic. The Hebrew frames Yeshua's teaching as musar — ethical wisdom instruction in the Proverbs tradition.

Uses בעל כח ('master of power' — ba'al koach) — a compound phrase meaning 'one who possesses authority.' Greek ἐξουσίαν ἔχων ('having authority'). The Hebrew בעל (ba'al — 'master/owner', H1167) implies ownership — he possesses power as its lord.

Uses חכמי הדת ('wise-ones of the law/religion') for scribes. Greek γραμματεῖς ('scribes/copyists'). The Hebrew is honorific — 'sages of the law'; the Greek is functional — 'writers.' A back-translator from Greek would use סופרים (sofrim — 'scribes'), not the respectful 'wise-ones of the law.'
translation_notes: 'Instruction' for musar preserves the Proverbs wisdom-teaching framework.
'Wise-ones of the law' for חכמי הדת — a respectful Hebrew designation for Torah scholars.

verses.translation: And there was{H1961} in the house of assembly a certain man{H120}, and he cried out{H6817}.

greek_deviations: Greek specifies ἄνθρωπος ἐν πνεύματι ἀκαθάρτῳ ('a man with an unclean spirit'). The Hebrew says only 'a man, and he cried out' — leaving the nature of his affliction to be revealed in dialogue. The Hebrew narration is more restrained.

verses.translation: And he said{H559}: What have you to do{H6213} with me, Yeshua{H3442} the Natsri? Have you come{H935} to destroy{H8045} us? I know{H3045} that you are the Holy One{H6918} of the Name{H8034}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses קדוש השם ('the Holy One of the Name', H6918+H8034) — where השם (HaShem — 'the Name') is the standard Jewish circumlocution for YHWH used to this day. Greek has ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ ('the Holy One of God'). A back-translator from Greek would write קדוש האלהים ('the Holy One of God'). The Hebrew uses the distinctly Jewish reverential substitute השם, which no translator working from Greek would independently produce.

Uses להשמיד (lehashmid — 'to destroy/annihilate', H8045) — the total-destruction verb for annihilating nations (Deut 2:21-22; 9:3; Josh 7:7). Greek ἀπολέσαι ('to destroy/ruin') is weaker. The Hebrew implies utter annihilation — the demonic realm fears complete obliteration.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Holy One of the Name' (HaShem). Greek: 'the Holy One of God.' Different divine reference.
translation_notes: 'The Name' preserves the Jewish circumlocution HaShem — the standard reverential way of referring to YHWH.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} rebuked{H1605} him, saying{H559}: Be silent! Come out{H3318} from that man{H120}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גערו (ga'aro — 'rebuked him', H1605) — the OT verb for divine rebuke over chaotic forces: YHWH rebukes the sea (Ps 106:9, Nah 1:4) and the adversary (Zech 3:2). The Hebrew places Yeshua's exorcism in the pattern of YHWH's cosmic authority.

verses.translation: And the adversary{H7854}, tormenting him, came out{H3318} from that man{H120}, screaming{H6817}. And all{H3605} were{H1961} astonished{H8539}.

greek_deviations: Greek: τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἀκάθαρτον ('the unclean spirit'). Hebrew: השטן ('the adversary/satan'). Different terminology — the Hebrew names the entity; the Greek describes its nature.
Hebrew places the crowd's astonishment here in v.26. Greek places it in v.27.

verses.translation: And they said{H559} one{H259} to another: What is this? A new{H2319} instruction{H4148}, which has power to command{H6680} the demons{H7700}, and they obey{H8085} him!

one_way_hebrew: Uses שדים (shedim — 'demons', H7700) — the specific OT term from Deut 32:17 ('they sacrificed to shedim, not to God') and Ps 106:37. Greek πνεύμασι τοῖς ἀκαθάρτοις ('unclean spirits'). A back-translator from Greek would write רוחות טמאות ('unclean spirits'), not the Torah-specific שדים.
Again uses מוסר (musar — 'instruction', H4148) — consistent Hebrew vocabulary maintaining the Proverbs wisdom framework.

verses.translation: And his fame{H8034} spread throughout all{H3605} Galil{H1551}.

translation_notes: שמו (shemo — 'his name/fame', H8034). In Hebrew, 'name' carries the sense of reputation and fame (Gen 6:4, 2 Sam 7:9).

verses.translation: And immediately when he came out{H3318} of the house of assembly, they came{H935} to the house{H1004} of Shimon{H8095} and Andri, with Yaakov{H3290} and Yochanan{H3110}, to eat{H398}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לאכול ('to eat', H398) — stating the purpose of the visit. Greek has no stated purpose — they simply enter the house. The Hebrew adds the practical, communal reason (eating together after Shabbat assembly) — a natural Hebrew narrative detail absent from Greek.

verses.translation: And the mother-in-law{H2545} of Kefa was lying{H7901} sick{H2470} with fever{H6920}, and immediately she told{H559} him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כיפא (Kefa — Aramaic 'rock') — switching from שמעון (Shimon) in v.29. This bilingual name-switching (Hebrew Shimon / Aramaic Kefa) is natural in a Hebrew-Aramaic milieu. Greek uses Σίμωνος ('Simon') consistently.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'she told him' (אמרה לו) — the mother-in-law speaks directly. Greek: 'they told him about her' (λέγουσιν αὐτῷ περὶ αὐτῆς) — others report her condition. Different agency.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} came{H935} and lifted{H5375} the hand{H3027}, and immediately the fever{H6920} left{H5800} her, and she served{H8334} them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ושרתם (vesheratem — 'and she served them', H8334) — again the Levitical ministry verb (שרת), used of priestly service in the sanctuary. Greek διηκόνει ('served/waited on') is generic. The Hebrew dignifies her act with priestly vocabulary.

verses.translation: And in the evening{H6153}, when the sun{H8121} was subdued, they sent{H7971} to him all{H3605} the sick{H2470} and the satan-possessed.

one_way_hebrew: Uses השמש נכנע ('the sun was subdued', H3665) — using the verb נכנע (nichna — 'was subdued/humbled'), the word for enemies being subdued before Israel (Deut 9:3, Judg 3:30, 1 Sam 7:13, 2 Chr 7:14). The sun 'submits' — a personification absent from Greek, which simply says ὅτε ἔδυ ὁ ἥλιος ('when the sun set'). No back-translator would choose this verb for 'setting.'

Uses משוטנים (meshotanim — 'satan-possessed') — a uniquely Hebrew term formed from שטן (satan), describing possession by the Adversary himself. Greek δαιμονιζομένους ('demon-possessed') uses a different concept entirely. The Hebrew category 'satan-possessed' does not exist in Greek vocabulary.
translation_notes: 'Satan-possessed' for meshotanim — a distinctive Hebrew coinage not found in the OT or in Greek.

verses.translation: And all{H3605} those from the city{H5892} were{H1961} gathered{H6908} before{H6440} the door{H6607}.
And many{H7227} came{H935} with various illnesses{H2483}, and many{H7227} satan-possessed. He drove out{H1644} the demons{H7700}, for they recognized{H5234} him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מגרש (megaresh — 'drove out', H1644, from גרש) — the verb for Adam being driven from Eden (Gen 3:24) and driving nations from the land (Ex 23:28-31, Deut 33:27). The Hebrew connects exorcism to the Edenic/conquest expulsion pattern.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'he did not allow the demons to speak, because they knew him' (οὐκ ἤφιεν λαλεῖν τὰ δαιμόνια). Hebrew gives only the reason: 'they recognized him.'

verses.translation: And he rose{H6965} in the morning{H1242} and went out{H3318} and walked{H1980} into the wilderness{H4057}, and there{H8033} he prayed{H6419}.
And Shimon{H8095} and those who were with him walked{H1980} after him{H310}.
And when they found{H4672} him, they said{H559} to him: All{H3605} the peoples{H5971} seek{H7592} you.

one_way_hebrew: Uses העמים (ha-amim — 'the peoples', H5971, plural) — implying multiple communities or ethnic groups. Greek πάντες ('everyone') is simply 'all.' The Hebrew plural 'peoples' may reflect the diverse population of Galilee.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: Let us go{H1980} to the towns and to the provinces{H4082} that surround{H5439} us, and let us proclaim{H1875} there{H8033}, for this is why I came{H935}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מדינות (medinot — 'provinces/districts', H4082) — the administrative term from Esther, Ezra, and Daniel for governmental regions. Greek κωμοπόλεις ('market-towns') is a uniquely Greek compound. A back-translator from Greek would use עיירות ('towns') or כפרים ('villages'), not the administrative מדינות.

verses.translation: And he was{H1961} proclaiming{H1875} in their houses of assembly and throughout all{H3605} Galil{H1551}, driving out{H1644} the demons{H7700} from the men{H376}.

greek_deviations: Greek: 'throughout all Galilee... and casting out demons' (general). Hebrew adds 'from the men' (מן האנשים) — specifying the source from which demons are expelled.

verses.translation: And a certain man{H120} came{H935} to him, a leper{H6879}, and bowed down{H6915} to him, saying{H559}: If{H518} you desire{H7521}, you are able to cleanse{H2891} me.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מצורע (metsora, H6879) — the specific Levitical term from Torah purity laws (Lev 13-14). The metsora is a precisely defined legal status requiring priestly examination. Greek λεπρός ('leper') is a medical term lacking the Levitical legal framework.
Uses ויקוד (vayiqod — 'bowed down', H6915) — deep prostration used before God (Gen 24:26, Ex 4:31, 34:8). Greek γονυπετῶν ('kneeling') is less intense — kneeling vs. full prostration.

Uses תרצה (tirtseh — 'you desire/delight in', H7521, from רצה) — the verb of God's acceptance of sacrifices (Lev 1:4, Ps 44:4, 51:18). Greek θέλῃς ('you wish') is simple volition. The Hebrew frames the request in sacrificial-acceptance language.
translation_notes: 'Desire' for tirtseh — capturing the Hebrew verb's sacrificial overtone.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442}, having compassion{H7355} upon him, sent out{H7971} his hand{H3027} and said{H559} to him: I desire{H7521} — be clean{H2889} from the leprosy{H6883}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כמרחם (ke-merachem — 'having compassion', H7355, from רחם) — the womb-compassion verb (Isa 49:15 — 'Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion — מֵרַחֵם — on the son of her womb?'; Ps 103:13). Greek σπλαγχνισθείς ('moved in the intestines') uses a different body metaphor. Some Greek manuscripts read ὀργισθείς ('being angry') instead.

Uses שלח ידו ('sent out his hand') — the OT idiom for divine power in action (Ex 3:20 — 'I will send out my hand'; Ex 7:5, 9:15). Greek ἐκτείνας τὴν χεῖρα ('stretching out the hand') is merely physical. The Hebrew phrase echoes God's hand in the Exodus.

verses.translation: And immediately he was cleansed{H2891}.
[He sent him out{H3318}.]

greek_deviations: Greek: ἐμβριμησάμενος αὐτῷ εὐθὺς ἐξέβαλεν αὐτόν ('having sternly warned him, he immediately sent him away'). The Hebrew preserves only the action, not the stern warning.
textual_notes: Brackets in the source indicate textual uncertainty or editorial reconstruction.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to him: Hear{H8085}! Tell{H559} no man{H120}, but go{H1980} and show yourself{H7200} to the deputies{H5461} of the priests{H3548}, and vow{H5087} for your cleansing{H2893} what Moshe{H4872} commanded{H6680}, for a witness{H5715} in Yisrael{H3478}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses סגני הכהנים ('deputies of the priests', H5461) — סגן is a Persian loanword for 'prefect/deputy' (Neh 2:16, 4:8,13; Jer 51:23,28,57). Greek τῷ ἱερεῖ ('the priest', singular). The Hebrew uses a specific Temple administrative title reflecting knowledge of the priestly bureaucracy. A back-translator from Greek would write הכהן ('the priest'), not 'deputies of the priests.'

Uses ותדור ('and vow', H5087, from נדר) — to make a vow. Greek προσένεγκε ('offer/bring near') means to present an offering. The Hebrew frames the cleansing requirement as a neder (vow) — a distinct OT institution (Lev 27; Num 30; Deut 23:22-24). A back-translator from Greek would use הקרב ('offer'), not תדור ('vow').

Uses לעדות בישראל ('for a witness in Yisrael') — the specifically national focus. Greek εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς ('for a testimony to them'). Different referent: 'in Yisrael' (the whole nation) vs. 'to them' (the priests).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'deputies of the priests' (plural administrative title). Greek: 'the priest' (singular).
Hebrew: 'vow' (נדר — a legal commitment). Greek: 'offer' (προσφέρω — a sacrificial act).
translation_notes: 'Deputies' for seganim — preserving the specific Temple administrative title.
textual_notes: The cleansing rite is prescribed in Leviticus 14:1-32 — involving two birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, hyssop, and priestly examination.

verses.translation: And when he went out{H3318}, he began to proclaim{H1875} and publicize the miracle{H5251}, until Yeshua{H3442} was not{H3808} able to enter{H935} a city{H5892} in hiding, but was compelled to remain{H5975} outside{H2351} in the wilderness{H4057}. And there{H8033} peoples{H5971} gathered{H6908} from all{H3605} sides.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נס (nes — 'miracle/sign/banner', H5251) — the OT word for a miraculous sign or rallying banner (Ex 17:15, Num 21:8-9, Isa 11:10). Greek τὸν λόγον ('the word/matter') is generic. The Hebrew identifies the healing as a nes — a sign in the Exodus tradition. A back-translator from Greek would write דבר ('word/matter'), not נס.

Uses בהחבא ('in hiding', from חבא — 'to hide', Gen 3:8,10). Greek φανερῶς εἰσελθεῖν ('to enter openly'). Hebrew: 'could not enter in hiding'; Greek: 'could not enter openly.' These are opposite conditions — the Hebrew says he sought concealment but couldn't achieve it.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the miracle' (הנס). Greek: 'the word/matter' (τὸν λόγον). Different content being publicized.
Hebrew: 'in hiding' (בהחבא — he tried to be hidden). Greek: 'openly' (φανερῶς — he tried to be open). Opposite perspectives.

chapter_notes.summary: Mark 1 in Hebrew uses distinctly Hebraic vocabulary throughout. Key one-way translation markers include: (1) קדוש השם ('Holy One of the Name') using the Jewish circumlocution HaShem where Greek has 'Holy One of God'; (2) ממלכות שמים ('kingdom of heaven') vs. Greek 'kingdom of God'; (3) כפרת ('atonement' — Yom Kippur language) where Greek has mere 'forgiveness'; (4) תשובה ('return') vs. Greek μετάνοια ('mind-change'); (5) נהגו ('led gently') vs. Greek ἐκβάλλει ('drove out') for the Spirit's action; (6) סגני הכהנים ('deputies of the priests') showing Temple bureaucratic knowledge; (7) שדים (shedim — Torah demons) vs. Greek 'unclean spirits'; (8) נס ('miracle/banner') vs. Greek 'word'; (9) משוטנים ('satan-possessed') as a uniquely Hebrew category; (10) חכמי הדת ('wise-ones of the law') vs. Greek 'scribes'; (11) מוסר ('Proverbs-style instruction') vs. Greek 'teaching.' The Hebrew consistently employs Levitical, priestly, and Torah-specific vocabulary where the Greek uses generic terms.
